Sam Yates has pulled every nuance out of Golden Boy.

But in a production as good as this one by Sam Yates and with a forceful central performance by Josh O’Connor as Joe Bonaparte, violinist turned boxer in Depression-era America, it makes its case as a powerful, admonitory slice of theatre noir.

O’Connor doesn’t pull his punches as he takes on the role of Joe Bonaparte, an ambitious and gifted violinist from an Italian American family, who abandons his true musical passions in favour of the fame and riches of boxing.
The last 20 minutes go slightly off the rails as the production's melodramatic denouement resorts to explosive bursts of shouting and recrimination following a bloody and tragic bout.
This boxing drama doesn’t so much pull its punches as fail to land its killer blows.
I love a boxing noir with its fast wise-cracking dialogue, and thought this was terrific.
This is a production that packs a powerful punch, resulting in what is confidently a knockout hit.
An outstanding revival of a playwright whose works should be far more visible.
For all the bluntness of Odets ’ writing, this production finds theatricality in the spaces where subtlety is absent — turning Golden Boy into something immediate, visceral and deeply affecting.

cn.t: O'Connor delivers a knockout performance in this pulpy Depression-era melodrama, though critics find Odets' 1937 play clunky and on-the-nose. Strong direction and ensemble work elevate the rarely-revived material into compelling theatre noir.
